claims.text: Kubernetes does not create the load balancer for a LoadBalancer Service: the API server stores it, and a controller watching such Services (on a cloud usually the provider's) sets one up and writes its address into the Service's status (.status.loadBalancer), shown as EXTERNAL-IP.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Concepts > Services > type: LoadBalancer ('on cloud providers which support external load balancers'; '.status.loadBalancer'); Components > cloud-controller-manager (service controller)

claims.text: A claim is fulfilled by the provisioner its StorageClass names. On a cloud the default StorageClass the cluster comes with usually names the provider's provisioner, which creates a network disk; it can be attached to another node within provider limits, such as one zone.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Concepts > Storage > Storage Classes (Provisioner, Volume binding mode / allowedTopologies); Persistent Volumes (Lifecycle: provisioning, binding)

claims.text: A cluster on machines you run yourself accepts the same manifests; without a component that answers LoadBalancer Services, EXTERNAL-IP stays <pending>, and a claim gets only what the StorageClasses already in the cluster provide; there may be none.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Services > type: LoadBalancer ('you must provide one'); Storage Classes; outline items 2-3

claims.text: kind runs no controller that hands out LoadBalancer addresses, so echo-loadbalancer shows <pending> under EXTERNAL-IP (still after 10 seconds in service-types.sh).
claims.source_hint: kind docs: LoadBalancer (needs cloud-provider-kind or another component); outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/service-types.txt; lesson k8s.l3.service-types claim 8

claims.text: kind's default StorageClass standard (provisioner rancher.io/local-path, WaitForFirstConsumer) creates each volume as a folder on the node chosen for the first Pod; the PersistentVolume's node affinity keeps later Pods on that node, so a new writer stays Pending while that node is unschedulable.

By default kind creates a Docker network named kind and attaches each node container to it; each node gets an address on it (172.22.0.x in the captured runs). Other containers, such as nodes of other kind clusters, may be attached too.
claims.source_hint: kind docs: Known Issues / Configuration (network 'kind'); outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/metallb-pool.txt ('the network kind: 172.22.0.0/16'); outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/cni.txt node addresses

claims.text: deploy/k8s/kind-config.yaml at stage-3 defines one control-plane and two worker nodes with the pinned node image and names no network, address range or storage.
kind installs on its own the CNI plugin kindnet and the default StorageClass standard in every cluster it builds by default.
claims.source_hint: kind docs (default CNI kindnetd; local-path-provisioner as default storage); lessons k8s.l3.cni-plugins, k8s.l2.storage-classes; outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/csi.txt

claims.text: echo-loadbalancer.yaml is a Service with type: LoadBalancer, selector app=echo-ip, port 80, targetPort 8080, in network-lessons; it names no component to answer the request.

Any component in the cluster that watches LoadBalancer Services and writes an address into their status can answer them; in the next lesson echo-loadbalancer on donhang gets an address from the kind network (172.22.255.202 in the capture).
docker network inspect kind --format '{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}} {{end}}' prints the names of the containers attached to the network kind.
claims.source_hint: docs.docker.com: docker network inspect (--format, Go template; Containers map with Name)

claims.text: kind names the node containers of cluster donhang donhang-control-plane, donhang-worker and donhang-worker2; kubectl get storageclass shows 'standard (default)' with provisioner rancher.io/local-path.
Components that replace the cloud's part (address handling, replicated storage) become the team's to run: their upgrades, failures and capacity, next to the cluster's own.
claims.source_hint: outline item 5; conditioned on the cluster running on machines without a provider

claims.text: A network disk lives outside every node and is reached over the network, so it can be attached to the node a Pod moves to.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Concepts > Storage > Persistent Volumes (network-attached storage, access modes)

claims.text: kind's default CNI plugin kindnet routes each node's Pod range via that node's address on the kind network, so plain routes between node addresses carry Pod traffic.
scripts/k8s/cluster-up.sh prints 'The cluster donhang already exists.' when kind get clusters lists donhang.
